system: You are an expert reviewer of machine-learning research ideas.
user:
Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: In MVFA's zero-shot (leave-one-modality-out) training, the segmentation adapters — the only part that produces anomaly maps — are trained with Dice and Focal losses exclusively on the three source datasets that have pixel masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), while OCT17, ChestXray and HIS only train the detection adapters. Primary question: can the segmentation adapters be trained from image-level labels alone, and how much mask-supervised localisation does that retain on the unseen modality? At each of the four adapter levels, with the original level weights, the Dice and Focal terms are replaced by an image-level BCE on the top-k mean of the level's patch-to-text anomaly probabilities (k = 1% of patches), applied to all five source datasets with every mask discarded; the detection adapters and their loss are unchanged. Hypothesis: because patch scores are similarities to text anchors shared by all modalities, this weak supervision yields localisation that transfers to the unseen modality. Primary outcomes: pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO on the held-out folds with masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) and image-level AUROC on all folds, mask-supervised versus image-label-supervised MVFA under the shared protocol. Secondary analyses: (i) a control in which the text anchors of the segmentation branch are replaced by a learned linear patch classifier trained with the same MIL loss, isolating the role of the text anchors; (ii) a per-level breakdown; (iii) two label-budget points with masks for 10% and 25% of the abnormal source images (one seed, two folds).

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Anatomy-debiased MIL under text and random anchor frames
SUMMARY: Train the segmentation adapters with top-k MIL plus hard-negative mining of the top-k patches of normal images, under MVFA's text anchors and under scale-matched random anchors, to test both whether debiasing improves weak localisation and whether its effect depends on the meaning of the anchors.
HYPOTHESIS: Normal hard-negative mining raises held-out pixel AUROC of MIL-trained segmentation adapters by at least 2 points over plain top-k MIL, and the gain is the same (within 1 point) under text and scale-matched random anchors, showing that it acts on the visual adapters rather than on anchor semantics.
RATIONALE: The anatomy parent identifies a concrete failure of MIL (top-k patches on salient anatomy) and corrects it with image labels alone; its positional prior is fragile on unaligned modalities, so only the hard-negative term is kept, which needs no alignment. The anchor-frame parent provides the control that separates the contribution of text meaning from that of a fixed frame and its scale. Combining them gives one improvement and one explanation in a 2 x 2 design whose cells are each one flag in the training script.
METHOD: 1) loss.py: mil_hardneg(p_l, label, k_frac=0.01, w_hard=2): abnormal images: BCE(top-k mean, 1); normal images: BCE on all patches towards 0 plus w_hard x BCE(top-k mean, 0). 2) utils.py: make_anchors('text' | 'rand'), random pair rescaled to the text pair's difference length, 3 draws. 3) train_zero.py: flags --loss {mil, mil_hardneg} --anchors {text, rand}. 4) Hyper-parameters: w_hard {1, 2, 4}; released learning rate and epochs.
EXPERIMENT: Leave-one-modality-out zero-shot training on BMAD (RESC and OCT17 held out together); all source masks discarded; checkpoints selected on source-modality validation by image AUROC; mask-supervised MVFA and the problem's plain top-k MIL re-run under the same rule; 3 seeds, mean and std; pixel AUROC and AUPRO on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC, image AUROC on all folds. 2 x 2 design (loss x anchors) plus mask-supervised MVFA with text anchors. Diagnostic: fraction of top-k patches of abnormal source images inside true masks. Falsified if hard negatives do not improve pixel AUROC, or if their gain differs by more than 1 point between frames.

Idea B:
TITLE: Consensus MIL with an anchor-frame control
SUMMARY: Train the segmentation adapters with cross-level consensus MIL under MVFA's text anchors and under scale-matched random anchors, testing whether consensus selection improves weak localisation and whether its benefit relies on the shared anchor frame rather than on the anchors' meaning.
HYPOTHESIS: Consensus MIL (top-k on the geometric mean of the four level maps) raises held-out AUPRO by at least 3 points over per-level MIL under both text and scale-matched random anchors, with a difference of less than 1 point between the two frames, whereas giving each level its own random frame removes at least half of the consensus gain.
RATIONALE: The consensus parent argues that the four levels' probabilities are comparable because they are read in one anchor frame; the anchor-control parent shows, following Do Words Matter?, that this frame matters through its geometry, not its words. Combining them makes the mechanism of consensus MIL testable: if the shared frame is what makes level agreement meaningful, scale-matched random anchors should work as well as text anchors, and separate random frames per level should break the consensus gain.
METHOD: 1) loss.py: consensus_mil as in the parent (geometric mean of level probabilities, top-k = 1%, selection detached; normal images: per-level top-k BCE towards 0). 2) utils.py: make_anchors('text' | 'rand' | 'rand_per_level'), random pairs rescaled to the text pair's difference length, 3 draws. 3) train_zero.py: flags --loss {mil, consensus} --anchors {text, rand, rand_per_level}. 4) Hyper-parameters: k_frac 1%; released learning rate and epochs.
EXPERIMENT: Leave-one-modality-out zero-shot training on BMAD (RESC and OCT17 held out together); all source masks discarded; checkpoints selected on source-modality validation by image AUROC; mask-supervised MVFA and the problem's plain top-k MIL re-run under the same rule; 3 seeds, mean and std; pixel AUROC and AUPRO on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC, image AUROC on all folds. Design: loss {per-level MIL, consensus} x anchors {text, shared random, per-level random}. Diagnostics: overlap of per-level top-k sets; fraction of selected patches inside true masks. Falsified if consensus does not beat per-level MIL, or if per-level random frames keep the full gain.

Respond in exactly this format:
REASONING: <one to three sentences explaining your choice>
CONFIDENCE: <HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW>
WINNER=<A | B | TIE>
